or unsupported capabilities once per session; record query failures and coverage

to that question. State the limitation and fallback to the user.

1	# Command-assembly split — per-cluster recipe
2	
3	Project trail: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2619 (one change per cluster).
4	Base branch for all wave-1 work: `cor-2268-cmdutil` (adds `internal/cli/internal/cmdutil` with WriteJSON/WriteText/WriteTextToWriter/StickyErrorWriter — use these, never copy them).
5	
6	## Goal per cluster
7	
8	Move one command cluster out of package `cli` into `internal/cli/command/<name>`
9	(package `<name>`), exporting `New(opts base.Options) *cobra.Command` (plus
10	additional constructors if the cluster registers several commands). The root
11	assembler (`internal/cli/root.go`) imports the package and mounts the command;
12	nothing else in `cli` may import the new package unless it already called the
13	moved code. The new package must NOT import `internal/cli`.
14	
15	## Layering (already in place — use it, do not re-create it)
16	
17	- `internal/cli/internal/base` — env/XDG/store paths (`base.EntireEnv`,
18	  `base.Options`, `base.ResolvePluginDirs`, `base.BrainDirForKey`), redaction,
19	  safe reads, agent args. `cli.Options`/`cli.EntireEnv` are aliases of these.
20	- `internal/cli/internal/brainstore` — locks, atomic writes, privacy state
21	  (tombstones, transactions, read guard, retrieval policy), untrusted state
22	  readers, error-code taxonomy (`brainstore.MemoryErrorCode`, `*Code` consts).
23	- `internal/cli/internal/cmdutil` — command output helpers.
24	- `internal/cli/internal/clitest` — `clitest.PinXDGRoots` (every new test
25	  package MUST have `main_test.go` with `func TestMain(m *testing.M) { os.Exit(clitest.PinXDGRoots(m)) }`),
26	  `clitest.UseHostXDGDataHome`, shared fakes.
27	- `internal/cli/internal/patterntest` — corpus fixtures incl. `OpenCorpusMutableDB`.
28	- `internal/cli/patterns`, `internal/cli/workspace`, `internal/cli/entities` —
29	  feature logic. `workspace.DefaultStore(env)` is the store constructor.
30	
31	## Hard rules (from COR-2268; violations have failed CI before)
32	
33	1. **Never edit `internal/cli/main_test.go`'s `TestMain` declaration** — its
34	   normalized source SHA-256 is pinned in
35	   `tools/ci-bench/windows-production/settings.json`. Other decls in that file
36	   are editable. Do not touch anything under `tools/ci-bench/`.
37	2. **Tests move, not rewritten**: identical assertions and fixtures. Allowed
38	   edits: package clause, imports, symbol qualification forced by the move, and
39	   re-pointing a root-command invocation to the cluster's own constructor when
40	   the test exercises only this cluster (`NewRootCommand(opts)` +
41	   `cmd.SetArgs([]string{"<cmd>", ...})` → `<name>.New(opts)` +
42	   `cmd.SetArgs([...])` without the leading command word — keep the change
43	   minimal and obvious). A test that exercises several commands or root routing
44	   stays in `cli`.
45	3. **No shims**: never leave a `cli`-side function/const/var that merely
46	   forwards to the moved one — sed-rename the call sites. Type ALIASES in `cli`
47	   are allowed when they cut churn. A `cli`-side wrapper is allowed only when
48	   it binds a real `cli`-private dependency (precedent: `verifyDerivedClean`).
49	4. **Hook-seam vars** (`var x = func(...)` swapped by tests) get exactly ONE
50	   home. If a moved function reads one, the var moves (exported) and every
51	   swap site is renamed.
52	5. **Shared helpers sink, they don't duplicate.** If the cluster needs a
53	   `cli`-private helper that other `cli` code also uses, move it to the right
54	   internal package (base/brainstore/cmdutil/patterns/workspace) and rename ALL
55	   call sites. If the closure is large (>3 unexported helpers that are not
56	   obviously storage/output/env), STOP and report instead of improvising.
57	6. Keep one home for constants; export only what remaining callers need.
58	7. Comments move verbatim; update only identifier spellings inside them.
59	
60	## Mechanical sequence
61	
62	1. `git fetch origin` then branch from `cor-2268-cmdutil`:
63	   `git checkout -b cor-2268-cmd-<name> cor-2268-cmdutil`.
64	2. Record before-inventory:
65	   `go test ./internal/cli -list '.*' | grep -c '^Test\|^Benchmark\|^Example\|^Fuzz'`
66	   and save the sorted name list to a file.
67	3. Map the closure first: for every symbol the cluster's files reference that
68	   lives elsewhere in `cli`, decide move / sink / stays-with-adapter. Use
69	   `entire graph impact --repo . --head --format json --symbol <sym>` for
70	   exported/shared symbols and grep for the rest; cite what you checked in the
71	   final report. Compile early and often.
72	4. `git mv` the cluster's prod files to `internal/cli/command/<name>/`, set the
73	   package clause, export the constructor(s) (`newXCommand` → `New`, extra
74	   commands keep descriptive exported names). Qualify base/brainstore/cmdutil/
75	   patterns/workspace imports. Update `root.go` to `<name>.New(opts)`.
76	5. Create `internal/cli/command/<name>/main_test.go` (clitest pin) BEFORE
77	   moving any test file. Then `git mv` the cluster's test files; apply only the
78	   allowed edits.
79	6. Build + vet loop: `go build ./... && go vet ./...` until clean; then
80	   `gofmt -w -s internal/`.
81	7. Reconcile inventory: after-lists for `./internal/cli` and the new package;
82	   the union of names must equal the before-list exactly (TestMain is not a
83	   runnable root). Report moved-root names.
84	8. Verify moved bodies: diff each moved test function against its pre-move body
85	   normalized only for the rename map; report IDENTICAL/DIFFERS per root.
86	9. Gates, all mandatory, report real output:
87	   - `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/cli/command/<name>`
88	   - focused `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/cli -run '<ClusterPattern>'`
89	   - `GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build ./...`
90	   - `python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tools/ci-bench/windows-production/tests -p 'test_*.py'`
91	   - `python3 -B tools/coverage/mutation_check.py`
92	   - full race suite `go test -race -p=1 ./... -count=1 -timeout=30m` (run it;
93	     if wall-clock is prohibitive in your environment, run
94	     `go test -race -count=1 -timeout=20m ./internal/cli` plus every other
95	     package, and SAY SO explicitly in the report).
96	10. Commit on your branch with explicit file paths (never `git add -A`), message
97	    `refactor(cli): move <name> command(s) into internal/cli/command/<name>`,
98	    ending with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
99	    Do NOT push, do NOT open PRs or trails — the orchestrator lands branches.
100	
101	## Report format (what you return)
102	
103	- Branch name + commit SHA.
104	- Moved files (prod/test), moved root names and count, inventory before/after
105	  numbers, body-comparison verdicts.
106	- Helpers sunk to shared packages (symbol → new home) with impact/grep evidence.
107	- Anything re-pointed from NewRootCommand (test name + one-line description).
108	- Gate results verbatim (pass/fail + durations). Anything skipped and why.
109	- Anything that did not fit the rules (left in cli, and why).

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Datadog

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

import re, subprocess, os, sys
cli = 'internal/cli'
syms = [l.split(': ')[1] for l in open('/tmp/probe-raw-syms.txt')] if False else None
# collect symbols from combined probe
raw = open('/tmp/probe-raw.txt').read()
syms = sorted(set(re.findall(r'undefined: ([A-Za-z0-9_]+)', raw)))
files = [f for f in os.listdir(cli) if f.endswith('.go')]
prod = [f for f in files if not f.endswith('_test.go')]
src = {f: open(os.path.join(cli,f)).read() for f in prod}
moving = {'facts_write_cmd.go','facts_read_cmd.go','facts_admin_cmd.go','verify_cmd.go'}
defpat = lambda s: re.compile(r'^(func|var|const|type)\s+'+s+r'\b|^\t?'+s+r'\s+=|^\t'+s+r'\s', re.M)
for s in syms:
    if s in ('Options','CommandRunner','EntireEnv'): continue
    deffile=[]
    callers=set()
    word=re.compile(r'\b'+s+r'\b')
    for f,txt in src.items():
        if not word.search(txt): continue
        if re.search(r'^func (\(\w+ [^)]+\) )?'+s+r'\(', txt, re.M) or re.search(r'^(var|type) '+s+r'\b', txt, re.M) or re.search(r'^\t'+s+r'\b[^=\n]*=', txt, re.M) or re.search(r'^const '+s+r'\b', txt, re.M) or re.search(r'^\t'+s+r'\s+(\w|=|\*)', txt, re.M) and ('const' in txt[:txt.find('\t'+s)][-400:] or True)==False:
            deffile.append(f)
        callers.add(f)
    stay = sorted(c for c in callers if c not in moving and c not in deffile)
    print(f"{s}\tDEF:{','.join(deffile) or '?'}\tSTAY-CALLERS:{len(stay)}\t{','.join(stay[:6])}")
EOF
python3 -I /tmp/callmap.py 2>&1 | head -120

1	package cli
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"errors"
6		"fmt"
7		"github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/cli/internal/cmdutil"
8		"os"
9		"path/filepath"
10		"strings"
11	
12		"github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/cli/internal/base"
13		"github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/cli/internal/factstore"
14		"github.com/spf13/cobra"
15	)
16	
17	// Facts that are not about one repository.
18	//
19	// Every fact a brain held belonged to a repo and a branch. That is right for
20	// most of them — "compaction runs above eight segments" is a claim about one
21	// codebase — and wrong for the rest. "I prefer table-driven tests", "we deploy
22	// on Thursdays", "the staging cluster is in eu-west-1" are true in every repo
23	// somebody works in, and had nowhere to live: record them in one repo's brain
24	// and they are invisible from the next, or record them in all of them and every
25	// correction has to be made N times.
26	//
27	// Worse, `remember` outside a repository failed outright. The one moment you
28	// most want to write something down — you are not in a checkout, you just
29	// learned something — was the one moment the command refused.
30	//
31	// A global brain is the same fact store in a different directory, sitting
32	// beside the per-repo ones. Reusing the store rather than inventing a second
33	// format means global facts get retraction, verification, taxonomy, dedupe and
34	// the write lock for free, and `facts` reads them with the code that already
35	// exists. Recall merges them in; everything else about them is ordinary.
36	
37	const (
38		// globalStoreDirName sits beside "repos" in the plugin data directory, so a
39		// global brain is visible next to the per-repo ones rather than buried
40		// inside one of them.
41		globalStoreDirName = "global"
42	
43		// globalFactBranch is the branch component of the global store's filename.
44		// Global facts are not on a branch; this is the storage layer's requirement,
45		// not a claim about the fact. Display never takes a fact's scope from this
46		// value — see globalFactIDs — because a repository may legitimately have a
47		// branch called "global" and a fact on it is not a global fact.
48		globalFactBranch = "global"
49	)
50	
51	// globalBrainDir returns the global store's directory, creating nothing. The
52	// caller creates it on first write, so merely reading never materialises a
53	// directory for somebody who has no global memories.
54	func globalBrainDir(env EntireEnv) (string, error) {
55		dirs, err := base.ResolvePluginDirs(env)
56		if err != nil {
57			return "", err
58		}
59		return filepath.Join(dirs.Data, globalStoreDirName), nil
60	}
61	
62	// loadGlobalFacts reads the global store. A store that does not exist yet is
63	// not an error: it is the state of every brain before the first global fact,
64	// and recall must not fail because of it.
65	func loadGlobalFacts(env EntireEnv) ([]factRecord, error) {
66		brainDir, err := globalBrainDir(env)
67		if err != nil {
68			return nil, err
69		}
70		if _, statErr := os.Stat(brainDir); statErr != nil {
71			if os.IsNotExist(statErr) {
72				return nil, nil
73			}
74			return nil, statErr
75		}
76		return factstore.Load(brainDir, globalFactBranch)
77	}
78	
79	// globalFactIDs is how the rest of the code knows which facts are global.
80	//
81	// Taking it from the records that were actually loaded out of the global store
82	// — rather than from a field on the fact — means the answer stays right no
83	// matter what a repository's branches are called, and no matter what a fact's
84	// stored branch says.
85	func globalFactIDs(facts []factRecord) map[string]bool {
86		ids := make(map[string]bool, len(facts))
87		for _, fact := range facts {
88			ids[fact.ID] = true
89		}
90		return ids
91	}
92	
93	// mergeGlobalFacts appends global facts to a repository's, dropping any whose
94	// id a repository fact already has.
95	//
96	// The repository's copy wins on a collision. Fact ids are content-derived, so a
97	// collision means the same statement is recorded in both places; the local one
98	// is the more specific claim and carries that repo's provenance, which is the
99	// evidence somebody would check.
100	func mergeGlobalFacts(repoFacts, global []factRecord) ([]factRecord, map[string]bool) {
101		// Only a live repository fact shadows. The precedence above is justified by
102		// the local copy being the more specific claim carrying checkable
103		// provenance; a retracted or superseded fact makes no claim, so it has
104		// nothing to shadow with. Letting it shadow anyway would mean retracting a
105		// local duplicate silently removed the global statement from this one repo.
106		seen := make(map[string]bool, len(repoFacts))
107		for _, fact := range repoFacts {
108			switch fact.Status {
109			case "", factStatusActive:
110				seen[fact.ID] = true
111			}
112		}
113		merged := repoFacts
114		globalIDs := map[string]bool{}
115		for _, fact := range global {
116			if seen[fact.ID] {
117				continue
118			}
119			// A retracted or superseded global fact is filtered by the same code
120			// that filters repository ones; nothing special happens here.
121			merged = append(merged, fact)
122			globalIDs[fact.ID] = true
123		}
124		return merged, globalIDs
125	}
126	
127	// globalFactsEnabled reports whether global facts should be merged into a
128	// repository read.
129	//
130	// Default on: a preference somebody recorded once is meant to apply, and a
131	// memory layer that makes you ask for what you already told it is not one.
132	// ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_GLOBAL_FACTS and --no-global turn it off, for a machine where
133	// repository answers must not be influenced by anything outside the repository.
134	func globalFactsEnabled(noGlobalFlag bool) bool {
135		if noGlobalFlag {
136			return false
137		}
138		return !base.SecurityToggleEnabled("ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_GLOBAL_FACTS")
139	}
140	
141	// globalFactsForRead loads the global store for a read surface, honouring the
142	// off switches. A damaged global store must not take retrieval down with it, so
143	// the error comes back for the caller to warn about rather than to propagate:
144	// the repository's own facts are still the answer to most queries.
145	func globalFactsForRead(env EntireEnv, noGlobal bool) ([]factRecord, error) {
146		if !globalFactsEnabled(noGlobal) {
147			return nil, nil
148		}
149		return loadGlobalFacts(env)
150	}
151	
152	// resolveGlobalFactsTarget is the global counterpart of resolveFactsTarget, for
153	// commands operating on the global store directly.
154	func resolveGlobalFactsTarget(env EntireEnv) (brainDir, branch string, err error) {
155		brainDir, err = globalBrainDir(env)
156		if err != nil {
157			return "", "", err
158		}
159		if err := os.MkdirAll(brainDir, 0o700); err != nil {
160			return "", "", fmt.Errorf("create global brain: %w", err)
161		}
162		return brainDir, globalFactBranch, nil
163	}
164	
165	// inARepository reports whether the current directory is actually inside a git
166	// working tree.
167	//
168	// It exists so `remember` outside a checkout can file the fact globally instead
169	// of refusing. The distinction matters: "you are not in a repository" is a
170	// reason to choose a different store, not a reason to throw away what somebody
171	// just typed.
172	//
173	// Asking git is the whole point, and the reason this does not simply check
174	// whether resolveFactsTarget succeeds: that succeeds for ANY directory that
175	// exists, then defaults the branch to "main" when git cannot name one. A fact
176	// recorded in ~/Desktop would be filed to a repository that does not exist, on
177	// a branch nobody is on, and never seen again — which is worse than the refusal
178	// this was meant to replace, because it looks like it worked.
179	// It returns an error for the case that is neither: a repository whose identity
180	// cannot be decided. resolveFactsTarget refuses to guess when state exists under
181	// two keys, and treating that refusal as "not in a repository" would swallow the
182	// guard and quietly file a repo-scoped fact globally — defeating the exact
183	// protection it was raised to provide. "No repository here" and "I cannot tell
184	// which repository this is" call for opposite responses.
185	func inARepository(ctx context.Context, opts Options) (bool, error) {
186		repoDir, _, _, err := resolveFactsTarget(ctx, opts, agentSurfaceTarget(opts, nil), "")
187		if err != nil {
188			var conflict *localRepoIdentityConflictError
189			if errors.As(err, &conflict) {
190				return false, err
191			}
192			return false, nil
193		}
194		inside, err := base.GitScalar(ctx, opts.Runner, repoDir, "rev-parse", "--is-inside-work-tree")
195		if err != nil {
196			return false, nil
197		}
198		return strings.TrimSpace(inside) == "true", nil
199	}
200	
201	// globalFactNotice is what the user sees when a fact was filed globally without
202	// them asking. Silence here would be the worst option: the fact is recorded
203	// somewhere they did not choose, and they would only find out by missing it.
204	func globalFactNotice(explicit bool) string {
205		if explicit {
206			return ""
207		}
208		return "not in a repository, so this was remembered globally; it will be recalled from every repo"
209	}
210	
211	// describeFactScope labels a fact for display.
212	func describeFactScope(fact factRecord, globalIDs map[string]bool) string {
213		if globalIDs[fact.ID] {
214			return "global"
215		}
216		return strings.TrimSpace(fact.Branch)
217	}
218	
219	// newFactsGlobalCommand lists what is in the global store.
220	//
221	// Global facts surface in every repository, which makes an unreviewable global
222	// store the worst kind: a wrong fact would follow somebody everywhere and there
223	// would be no one place to go and look at what they had accumulated. `recall`
224	// shows the ones matching a query; this shows all of them.
225	func newFactsGlobalCommand(opts Options) *cobra.Command {
226		var (
227			jsonOut    bool
228			includeAll bool
229		)
230		cmd := &cobra.Command{
231			Use:   "global",
232			Short: "List memories recorded globally rather than for one repository",
233			Args:  cobra.NoArgs,
234			RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, _ []string) error {
235				facts, err := loadGlobalFacts(opts.Env)
236				if err != nil {
237					return err
238				}
239				active := make([]factRecord, 0, len(facts))
240				for _, fact := range facts {
241					if !includeAll && fact.Status != "" && fact.Status != factStatusActive {
242						continue
243					}
244					active = append(active, fact)
245				}
246				brainDir, dirErr := globalBrainDir(opts.Env)
247				if dirErr != nil {
248					return dirErr
249				}
250				if jsonOut {
251					return cmdutil.WriteJSON(cmd, map[string]any{
252						"store": brainDir,
253						"count": len(active),
254						"facts": active,
255					})
256				}
257				out := cmd.OutOrStdout()
258				if len(active) == 0 {
259					// The empty state is where somebody learns the feature exists,
260					// so it says how to use it rather than only that there is
261					// nothing here.
262					fmt.Fprintln(out, "no global memories")
263					fmt.Fprintln(out, "  `entire-brain remember \"<memory>\" --global` records one for every repository")
264					return nil
265				}
266				for _, fact := range active {
267					printFactLine(out, fact)
268				}
269				fmt.Fprintf(out, "\n%d global memory(ies) in %s\n", len(active), brainDir)
270				return nil
271			},
272		}
273		cmd.Flags().BoolVar(&jsonOut, "json", false, "Emit the memories as JSON")
274		cmd.Flags().BoolVar(&includeAll, "all", false, "Include retracted and superseded memories")
275		return cmd
276	}

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.
